question.text: Mrs. Kavitha, an NRI client based in Singapore, earns Rs.12,00,000 as dividend income from Indian equities. The India-Singapore DTAA prescribes a withholding tax rate of 15% on dividends, while the Indian Income Tax Act prescribes 20%. She has a valid Tax Residency Certificate from Singapore and Form 10F. As her investment adviser, what should you recommend?

answer.text: She must pay 20% tax under the IT Act as domestic law always overrides DTAA provisions
She should pay 15% under the DTAA and additionally 5% under the IT Act to cover the differential

She should claim the DTAA rate of 15% on dividends as it is more beneficial than the IT Act rate, since a non-resident eligible for DTAA benefits is taxed under the DTAA or the Income Tax Act, whichever is more beneficial
She cannot claim DTAA benefits as an NRI since DTAAs apply only to foreign nationals, not Indian citizens residing abroad

explanation.text: The Logic: Per pages 217-218, where India has a DTAA with another country, a non-resident eligible for DTAA benefits is taxed under the DTAA or the Income Tax Act, whichever is more beneficial. Per page 228, dividend income of a non-resident is taxed under the Act or the relevant DTAA, whichever is more beneficial. Since the DTAA rate (15%) is lower than the IT Act rate (20%), Mrs. Kavitha should opt for the DTAA rate. The Trap: Domestic law does not automatically override the DTAA — the taxpayer gets the more beneficial of the two. There is no requirement to pay a "differential". DTAA benefits are available based on tax residency, not citizenship; an NRI who is a tax resident of a DTAA country can claim benefits. Note: Per page 218, in addition to a valid TRC, Form 10F is also required to claim DTAA relief. Both prerequisites should be in place before applying the beneficial rate.
